h: From the Stone Age to a Roman villa
p: Butser's buildings cover a huge sweep of time, so it's worth getting your head round the timeline before you start exploring. Some reconstructions are based on Neolithic houses, built by the very first farmers in Britain, while the big Iron Age roundhouses are probably the most famous and give a real sense of how spacious and cosy these homes could be. There's also a Roman villa building and an Anglo-Saxon hall, so you can walk through thousands of years of British history in an afternoon.

Pay attention to the smaller details too. The ancient crop varieties growing in the fields, the old breeds of animals and the experiments with things like storing grain in pits are all part of the archaeology going on here. Kids love comparing the houses and deciding which one they'd most like to live in, so it's a great way to get them thinking about how people adapted over time.

Look at the event calendar before you go. Seasonal festivals, often linked to old celebrations of the farming year, as well as craft workshops and archaeology days, can make a visit really memorable. These can be popular, so planning ahead pays off.

Right next door, the Queen Elizabeth Country Park and Butser Hill offer excellent walks, with chalk grassland, woodland and sweeping views across Hampshire. The market town of Petersfield is just up the A3, with a pretty heath and lake that's perfect for a stroll, and Portsmouth's historic dockyard is close enough to turn a weekend into a real history marathon.
